name: metapool
workload: Construction and reserve() of mtp::vault (pool-backed dynamic array) vs std::vector (std::allocator/ptmalloc) and std::pmr::vector (pmr pool + monotonic_buffer_resource), across element counts.
claimed_speedup: up to ~1300x faster construction/reserve than std::vector (std::allocator); up to ~3.5x faster than std::pmr::vector (pool resource)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8840U, Arch Linux kernel 6.15.8, glibc 2.42 (ptmalloc), 64GB DDR5
tradeoffs: Compile-time fixed pool layout (metaset) must be tuned per workload; no general fallback beyond configured strides; header-only but requires C++23; cannot grow arbitrarily beyond the preallocated arena without a reset.
caveats: The ~1300x figure comes from a narrow construction+reserve microbenchmark (bypassing malloc/realloc growth entirely), not sustained alloc/free churn; the ~3.5x-vs-pmr figure is more representative of general use. New project (created Aug 2025), 37 stars, no independent third-party verification found.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'C++ pool allocator faster than std::allocator benchmark github'

name: Hoard
baseline: Solaris default allocator, Ptmalloc (glibc malloc backing operator new/delete)
workload: Uniprocessor and multiprocessor (1-14 way Sun Enterprise 5000) allocation-intensive benchmarks: threadtest, shbench, Larson server simulation, active/passive false-sharing tests, BEMengine PDE solver, Barnes-Hut n-body solver, plus single-threaded espresso/Ghostscript/LRUsim/p2c.
claimed_speedup: Up to 60x over the standard Solaris allocator and up to 18x over the next-best allocator (Ptmalloc) at 14 processors (paper abstract); threadtest 278% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; shbench 85% faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; Larson 18x faster than Ptmalloc at 14 procs; BEMengine 10.6% faster than Solaris allocator uniprocessor
compiler_and_flags: GNU C++ at -O6 (Sun Workshop C++ compiler 5.0 used only for Barnes-Hut)
hardware: Sun Enterprise 5000, 2GB RAM, 14x 400MHz UltraSPARC CPUs, 4MB L2 cache, Solaris 7
stars_or_usage: 1.25k stars; historically used by AOL, Cisco, SAP, Reuters, RBC and others per README; standard allocator option in SPEC CPU2006
tradeoffs: Multi-heap design trades some memory for scalability (bounded blowup, not zero); link-time/LD_PRELOAD drop-in malloc replacement, not a std::allocator template adapter; per-processor heap hashing can cause heap/thread collisions.
caveats: Primary quantitative evidence is a peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2000 paper run on 26-year-old hardware (UltraSPARC/Solaris 7) against the Solaris and Ptmalloc allocators of that era, not a modern libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL build; no current reproduction with stated modern compiler/flags/hardware was found this session, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The GitHub repo itself is actively maintained in 2026 as a drop-in malloc replacement, and Hoard is also included (as 'hd') in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite, though that page's results are chart images only, not text numbers.
found_via: GitHub: found via daanx/mimalloc-bench README allocator list ('hd' = Hoard); followed citation to the ASPLOS 2000 paper

name: smmalloc
workload: Multi-threaded (1-5 threads on Windows/i7-2600; 1-4 threads on PS4) small-object alloc/dealloc stress test measuring total operations completed, comparing smmalloc against CRT malloc, rpmalloc, Hoard, ltalloc, dlmalloc.
claimed_speedup: ~40 cycles/op with thread cache; ~3.9x faster than CRT single-threaded (92.6M vs 23.9M ops) and ~2.6x faster at 5 threads (38.3M vs 14.6M ops) on i7-2600; ~8.1x faster than CRT single-threaded on PS4 (36.1M vs 4.4M ops)
stars_or_usage: 335 stars; shipped in Warface (PS4, Xbox One, Switch)
tradeoffs: Proxy allocator: only handles configured small-size buckets, passes everything else through to a fallback allocator; requires explicit per-thread cache create/destroy calls; not a drop-in std::allocator without a wrapper.
caveats: README benchmark states hardware but not compiler or optimization flags, so capped at Tier C rather than A/B; numbers are raw op counts from the project's own charts/tables, not independently reproduced. No commits since 2023.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'smmalloc SergeyMakeev small object allocator benchmark faster than malloc'

name: rpmalloc
baseline: operator new/delete (default malloc); also compared against tcmalloc, jemalloc, lockfree-malloc, Hoard, ptmalloc3
workload: Multi-threaded interleaved allocation/deallocation benchmark (random and fixed sizes 16B-160000B range, with cross-thread deallocation), measuring memory operations per CPU-second across thread counts.
claimed_speedup: rpmalloc faster than all tested allocators except lockfree-malloc in some high-thread-count cases; tcmalloc and jemalloc trail ~15% behind in performance
hardware: 8-core (4 physical + HT) Windows 10 / Linux (Ubuntu 16.10) machine, 12GiB RAM; 2-core MacBook, 8GiB RAM for macOS (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Malloc replacement (override new/delete or LD_PRELOAD), not a std::allocator template; thread-caching adds roughly 10-15% memory overhead vs some allocators.
caveats: Benchmark is the project's own suite; exact CPU model is not named (only core count/RAM), and compiler/optimization flags are not stated in BENCHMARKS.md, so capped at Tier C. Also appears as a strong performer in the independent daanx/mimalloc-bench suite (as 'rp'), though that page's numeric results are only in chart images, not text.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'rpmalloc benchmark vs malloc vs mimalloc vs tcmalloc github'

name: ltalloc
workload: Same multi-threaded small-object alloc/dealloc stress test used in the smmalloc benchmark table (Windows/i7-2600 and PS4), comparing ltalloc's throughput against CRT malloc.
claimed_speedup: ~2.6x faster than CRT single-threaded (62.5M vs 23.9M ops) on i7-2600; ~6.4x faster than CRT single-threaded on PS4 (28.6M vs 4.4M ops)
tradeoffs: Overrides global operator new/delete directly (not a std::allocator wrapper); best suited for many small (<256B) allocations; peak performance relies on LTO/inlining of the size-class computation.
caveats: Numbers are from a third-party project's (smmalloc) own comparison table, not from ltalloc's own README, which has no quantified benchmark of its own (only asm-output examples). Hardware is stated but compiler/flags are not, capping this at Tier C. Despite the 'r-lyeh-archived' org name and GitHub 'archived' fork lineage, the repo has commits in 2026 and is not GitHub-archived.
found_via: GitHub: harvested from SergeyMakeev/smmalloc README benchmark table while researching smmalloc

name: arena-allocator (ShortAlloc)
baseline: operator new/delete (GNU/glibc malloc via std::vector's default std::allocator)
workload: std::vector<TestClass>::emplace_back of 100 objects of sizes 8B-8KB, using a stack-backed bump-pointer Arena + ShortAlloc STL allocator vs the default heap allocator, measured on QuickBench (AWS-hosted).
claimed_speedup: Stack/arena allocator 2.2x-4.4x faster for objects up to 512B, and 93x-230x faster for 1KB-8KB objects (crossing glibc's mmap threshold)
hardware: QuickBench-hosted AWS machine pool; CPU model and load unstated (README includes explicit disclaimer that absolute QuickBench timings are unreliable)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars; featured in a Hacker News 'Show HN' post
tradeoffs: Bump allocator: cannot free individual objects out of order, only the whole arena at once (or most-recent-first); backed by a fixed-size std::array, so capacity is bounded by the configured arena size; not thread-safe.
caveats: Compiler and optimization flags are not stated, and several ratios (93x-230x) exceed the 50x implausibility threshold, coinciding with crossing glibc's mmap allocation threshold (a known artifact of that one size range, not a general allocator speed claim) -- capped at Tier C rather than A. QuickBench's own disclaimer says absolute durations on its shared AWS pool are 'meaningless' beyond relative comparison. No LICENSE file in the repo, so usability is 'reference' only, not 'copyable'.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'arena allocator C++ github faster than operator new' -> Hacker News 'Show HN: C++ Arena Allocator That's 200x+ Faster Than GNU Malloc'
